findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is in one plain sentence. Nothing else on the page shows the features it names: there is no request, no second-model check and no cost figure for this study.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. It shows how it read the request, has one AI model do the work and a different one check it, and records what each step cost.

findings.text: A link to the next step sits right in the header, so a newcomer who only wants to try Athena does not have to scroll through the whole study to find out what to do.
findings.source: Next step: install Athena or read firstmate itself.

findings.text: Next steps gives commands to install and try Athena. It assumes the reader already has a checkout, gives no clone command, and lists no requirements (for example a Rust toolchain or model API keys), so the reader has to go to the repository anyway.
findings.source: Next steps: "Install Athena from a checkout of its repository: ./setup.sh" and "Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog""

findings.text: This is Athena's home page, but almost all of it describes a different project, firstmate. A newcomer who came to learn about Athena gets three short paragraphs and then a long, dense specification of a tool they may never use.
findings.source: Page title "Athena explains how firstmate handles work" and the sections States, Counters, Transitions, Why it is built this way, Claims and sources

findings.text: This sentence is the page's only case for why Athena matters: the study is offered as proof. The page never says why traced claims would help the reader or who Athena is meant for, so a newcomer has to work out the value for themselves.
findings.source: Athena made this study of firstmate to show that it can read an unfamiliar project and explain it with every statement traced to a claim, and every claim to lines in the project's own files.

findings.text: "Words used first" says it defines the words in the sentences that follow, but it leaves out ship, scout, relaunch and secondmate, which the first summary list uses. The reader has to jump to the Glossary to follow the opening section.
findings.source: What firstmate is: "A ship changes a project; a local-only ship has no PR and lands by a guarded fast-forward. A scout produces a report and never a PR. A relaunch replaces a stuck worker with a new one."

findings.text: The Counters section names transitions by id (t1, t3, ...) before the Transitions section defines them, so the reference means nothing on a first read.
findings.source: Counters: "places-held, changed by transitions t1, t3, t4, t9, t11"

findings.text: The page says the same things many times: exit 75, places freed by a recorded PR, and the captain-call reopen each appear in Start here, the cards, the design choices and the Glossary. That makes the page long and harder to skim.
findings.source: Start here and the Transitions cards (e.g. t2: "the spawn is deferred with exit 75 and the item stays queued")

findings.text: Being open about what the sources do not say, here and in "Limits of this study", supports the trust claim. It also leaves a reader unsure about a key part of the yolo merge rule.
findings.source: in scope: "The cited instruction does not say what makes work in scope, so this page gives no test for it."

findings.text: Every claim links to exact lines at a pinned commit, so a sceptical reader can check any statement for themselves. This is the strongest proof the page gives of what Athena does.
findings.source: Next steps: "Check a statement: follow a bracketed claim id to the claim, then its source link to the file and lines in firstmate at the pinned commit."
